slides.title: Mechatronics: mechanical + electronic + computer
slides.body:
**Mechatronics**: integration of mechanical + electrical + computer engineering. Modern complex products are inherently mechatronic — every car, robot, drone, appliance, factory automation.

Key disciplines:
- **Mechanical**: kinematics, dynamics, structures.
- **Electrical**: sensors, actuators, power electronics.
- **Embedded software**: real-time control algorithms.
- **Systems engineering**: requirements + integration + testing.

**Examples**:
- **Car**: chassis (mech) + electric motors + ECUs + sensors (radar, camera, IMU) + software.
- **Industrial robot**: mechanical arm + servo motors + drivers + controller + force/vision sensors + path planner.
- **CNC machine**: spindle + axes + drives + encoders + CNC controller + CAM.
- **Drone**: propellers + motors + ESCs + IMU + GPS + flight controller + telemetry.
- **Surgical robot**: 4-7 DOF arms + tactile sensors + haptic feedback + control software.

**Sensors + actuators**: the mechatronic interfaces.

**Sensors**: measure physical quantities.
- **Position**: encoders (incremental, absolute), LVDT, potentiometer, resolver.
- **Velocity**: tachometer, derived from position.
- **Acceleration**: IMU (MEMS accelerometer), piezo.
- **Force**: load cells, strain gauges.
- **Torque**: torque sensors, current-based estimation.
- **Temperature**: thermocouple, RTD, thermistor.
- **Pressure**: piezo, MEMS, strain-gauge based.
- **Vision**: cameras (RGB, depth, IR, thermal).
- **Range**: LIDAR, ultrasonic, radar, time-of-flight.
- **Voltage/current**: shunts, Hall-effect, transformers.

**Actuators**: convert electrical to mechanical.
- **DC motors**: brushed (cheap, simple); brushless (BLDC, more efficient, longer life).
- **AC motors**: induction (industrial); synchronous (servo).
- **Stepper motors**: open-loop position. Used in 3D printers, CNC.
- **Servomotors**: closed-loop position + speed + torque. Robotics, machine tools.
- **Linear motors**: direct linear motion. Maglev, semiconductor steppers.
- **Pneumatic/hydraulic actuators**: high force/density. Heavy machinery.
- **Solenoids**: simple on/off motion. Valves, latches.
- **Piezoelectric**: high precision, low displacement. Atomic-force microscopes, fuel injectors.
- **Shape-memory alloys, MEMS**: specialized.

**Power electronics**: convert + control electrical power.
- Motor drivers (H-bridge, 3-phase inverter).
- DC-DC converters.
- AC-DC + DC-AC.
- SiC + GaN devices for high efficiency.

slides.title: Feedback control + PID
slides.body:
**Feedback control**: measure output, compare to setpoint, adjust input.

Loop:
```
setpoint → [error = sp - measured] → controller → actuator → plant → output → measurement → (feedback)
```

**Open-loop**: no feedback. Simple but poor tracking + disturbance rejection.

**Closed-loop**: feedback. Better tracking, robust to disturbances + parameter changes.

**PID controller**: most-used industrial controller. Output:
$$u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int e \, dt + K_d \frac{de}{dt}$$

Where $e(t) = r(t) - y(t)$ = error.

- **P (proportional)**: respond to current error. Stronger response = larger $K_p$. Too high = oscillation.
- **I (integral)**: respond to accumulated error. Eliminates steady-state offset. Too high = instability.
- **D (derivative)**: respond to RATE of error change. Damps oscillation. Sensitive to noise.

**Tuning PID**:
- **Ziegler-Nichols**: classical method. Set $K_i = K_d = 0$; raise $K_p$ until oscillation; back off + add I + D.
- **Manual tuning**: by trial + observation.
- **Auto-tuning**: many modern controllers do this.
- **Adaptive tuning**: continuously adjust gains.
- **Model-based**: identify plant model, design controller via control theory.

**Beyond PID**:
- **State-space control**: model plant as state equations $\dot{x} = Ax + Bu$; design controller via pole placement, LQR.
- **Model predictive control (MPC)**: optimize over future trajectory at each step. Excellent for multi-input + constraints. Used in process control + autonomous driving.
- **Adaptive control**: estimate plant parameters online + adjust controller.
- **Robust control**: account for plant uncertainty (H-infinity, etc.).
- **Optimal control**: minimize cost function (Pontryagin's principle).
- **Nonlinear control**: sliding mode, backstepping, feedback linearization.
- **Reinforcement learning** (modern): learn controller from data.

**Stability analysis**:
- **Bode plot**: frequency response. Margin of stability.
- **Nyquist criterion**: stability from open-loop response.
- **Root locus**: pole movement as gain changes.
- All taught in undergrad control theory.

**Practical implementation**:
- Sampling time: must be fast vs system dynamics (typically 10-100× faster).
- Anti-windup: integral term capping.
- Noise filtering on D term.
- Feed-forward + reference shaping for tracking.
- Saturation handling.

slides.title: Real-time embedded control + the modern stack
slides.body:
**Real-time control**: deterministic execution. Late = bad. Discussed in embedded-systems path; here for application.

**Control loops** at various rates:
- **Current/torque** (innermost): 10-100 kHz (motor PWM).
- **Velocity**: 1-10 kHz.
- **Position**: 100 Hz - 1 kHz.
- **Path/trajectory**: 10-100 Hz.
- **Mission/supervisory**: 1-10 Hz.

**Hardware**:
- Microcontroller (Cortex-M, ESP32, AVR).
- FPGA for fastest loops (sub-microsecond).
- DSP for signal processing.
- Industrial: PLC (Programmable Logic Controller). Real-time + reliable. Allen-Bradley, Siemens, Schneider.
- Safety-rated: redundant + diagnostic for safety-critical (robotics, automotive).

**Communication**:
- **CAN bus**: automotive + industrial. Robust + simple.
- **EtherCAT**: real-time Ethernet. Industrial automation.
- **PROFINET, EtherNet/IP**: factory automation.
- **Modbus**: legacy industrial. Still widespread.
- **MQTT, OPC-UA**: higher-level + cloud-connected.

**Modern trends**:
- **Drive integrated**: motor + driver + controller in one package. Easy plug-and-play.
- **Industrial Ethernet**: replacing fieldbus. Better bandwidth + integration.
- **Edge computing**: ML inference on factory floor. NVIDIA Jetson, Intel NUC, Coral.
- **Digital twins**: virtual replicas for simulation, training, optimization.
- **MTConnect, OPC-UA**: standardized data exchange.
- **Predictive maintenance**: ML on sensor data → predict failures before they happen.
- **Cobots (collaborative robots)**: human-safe without cages. Universal Robots, ABB YuMi, Fanuc CRX.

**Software stacks**:
- **Real-time OS**: FreeRTOS, Zephyr, vxWorks, QNX. Determinism.
- **ROS2 (Robot Operating System)**: middleware for robotics. DDS-based messaging.
- **PLC ladder + structured text**: industrial automation.
- **Simulink + Embedded Coder**: model-based control development.

**Industry 4.0 / Industrial IoT**: factory floor → cloud. Data-driven optimization, predictive maintenance, distributed manufacturing. Continuing growth.

**Autonomous systems**: cars (Waymo, Cruise, Tesla), drones, ships (Sea-Kit, Saildrone), space (Mars rovers, lunar landers). All deeply mechatronic. ML augmenting classical control.

question.question: Tune a PID for motor speed control
question.goal: DC motor, speed setpoint 1000 RPM. Step response: with $K_p$ alone (P-only), system reaches 950 RPM steady-state (slow response, error offset). With higher $K_p$: oscillates. What to do?

steps.prompt: Steady-state offset (50 RPM short of setpoint) suggests need for...

options: INTEGRAL term: $K_i \int e dt$. Accumulates error over time, eventually drives output to setpoint. Eliminates steady-state offset.

steps.reveal: Add integral term. Steady-state offset = no I action. Adding I will integrate the error + drive it to zero.

steps.prompt: With P + I, transient response may overshoot. Add D term?

options: Add derivative: $K_d de/dt$. Responds to RATE of error change → applies braking when error decreasing rapidly. Damps overshoot + oscillation. Common: PD or PID for smoother response.

steps.reveal: Add derivative for damping. PID complete. Tune: start with Ziegler-Nichols or manually adjust. Modern controllers auto-tune.

steps.prompt: If load varies (e.g., motor drives a saw cutting wood with varying thickness), what would help?

options: Feed-forward: anticipate load + add control effort in proportion. Or adaptive control: change gains based on operating regime. PID alone has finite disturbance rejection.

steps.reveal: Feed-forward or adaptive control. For known disturbance pattern: feed-forward. For unknown but slow: adaptive gains. For fast unknown: robust control. Modern: ML-augmented PID, learning the load model from data.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{PID = current error + accumulated + rate of change}}$$ PID is the workhorse industrial controller. Decades of theory + practice. ~95% of industrial control loops are PID variants. Beyond: MPC for constrained multi-input; adaptive + ML-based for complex/uncertain plants; sliding mode + robust for safety-critical. Foundational understanding of feedback control is essential mechatronic-engineer skill.

question.question: A new industrial robot programmer notices the arm vibrates when moving fast. Likely cause + fix?
options: Insufficient damping in control loop OR high $K_p$ relative to plant dynamics. Increase $K_d$ (damping), reduce $K_p$, OR add motion-profile shaping (smooth acceleration). Modern robots use feed-forward + reference-shaping for high-speed smooth motion.
question.explanation:
Vibration at speed = under-damped control. Fixes: (1) Higher $K_d$ (damping); (2) Lower $K_p$ (less aggressive); (3) Smoother trajectory (S-curve velocity profile vs trapezoidal); (4) Feed-forward (compensate inertial torque before error feedback corrects); (5) Notch filter at vibration frequency (mechanical resonance).

Modern industrial robots (ABB, FANUC, KUKA, UR) use combinations: PID + feed-forward + notch filters + reference shaping for smooth high-speed motion. Mechanical resonances + flexibility limit how fast you can go before vibration.

slides.workedSolution: Vibration: under-damped, gains too high, mechanical resonance, sharp velocity transitions. Fixes: tune PID gains, smooth trajectory, feed-forward (anticipate inertia), notch filter (kill resonance frequency). All these used in modern industrial robotics. Tracking + smoothness + speed are three competing objectives the control engineer balances.

question.prompt: Walk through the mechatronic stack: drive motors + battery + IMU + LIDAR + cameras + onboard computer + ROS + safety + cloud-connectivity.
Explain in two or three sentences why PID remains the most-used industrial controller despite advances in control theory.
question.rubric: Mentions that PID is simple, well-understood, tunable + reliable; works well for most single-loop applications without requiring a plant model; many advanced controllers (MPC, adaptive, robust) require modeling + more compute + more risk. Industrial practice values reliability + maintainability; PID delivers. Advanced control finds its niche in specific high-value cases (chemical process control, satellite attitude, autonomous driving), not general factory automation.
